Saith
seth
v. (third person singular present of say; rendering Hebrew 'amar and ne'um, Greek legei)
From Saxon sægþ, the third person singular present of secgan, to say. It is the older says, and in the Authorized Version it is above all the verb of the prophetic formula — Thus saith the LORD — which occurs some four hundred times.

Biblical Definition

Saith is the third person singular present of say, and its great office in Scripture is the messenger formula of the prophets. Thus saith the LORD is not a preface the prophet chose; it is the credential of a herald who carries another man's words and may not alter them. Jeremiah uses it to contradict the whole national mood: “Thus saith the LORD; Deceive not yourselves, saying, The Chaldeans shall surely depart from us: for they shall not depart” (Jeremiah 37:9). Ezekiel uses it to pronounce a sentence no man would invent (Ezekiel 35:14). And at the summit of the Abrahamic covenant the LORD swears by Himself with the same verb: “By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD” (Genesis 22:16). The present tense matters. The prophets do not say the LORD said, as though reporting an old communication, but saith — the word is being spoken now, and the hearer stands under it now. The Gospels use the same form for Christ's living speech: “he saith unto them, Our friend Lazarus sleepeth” (John 11:11). Scripture is not a record of what God once said; it is what God says.

Webster 1828 Definition

The third person singular of the present tense of say; the older form of says. In Scripture it is the verb of the prophetic messenger formula, Thus saith the LORD, and of Christ's own living speech in the Gospels.

expand to see more

SAITH, v. [Sax. sægþ.] The third person singular of the present tense of say; contracted in modern usage to says.

2. To speak; to utter in words; to declare.

3. In the prophetic writings it introduces the words of God delivered by a messenger; as, Thus saith the LORD.

4. It is retained in the solemn style and throughout the common version of the Scriptures.

5. In Scripture, By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD, Gen. 22; Thus saith the LORD; Deceive not yourselves, Jer. 37.

Key Scripture

Genesis 22:16 — "And said, By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD, for because thou hast done this thing, and hast not withheld thy son, thine only son:"

Jeremiah 37:9 — "Thus saith the LORD; Deceive not yourselves, saying, The Chaldeans shall surely depart from us: for they shall not depart."

Ezekiel 35:14 — "Thus saith the Lord GOD; When the whole earth rejoiceth, I will make thee desolate."

John 11:11 — "These things said he: and after that he saith unto them, Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep."

Modern Corruption

The formula Thus saith the LORD is claimed today by men who have received no such word — the modern prophet, the impression taken for revelation, the leader who baptises his own preference in the language of Sinai. The canon is closed, and the formula belongs to Scripture.

expand to see more

The New Apostolic Reformation and the wider charismatic prophecy movement have restored the formula without restoring its terms. In Scripture a prophet who spoke presumptuously in the LORD's name was to die, and the test was absolute accuracy; no allowance was made for a word that was mostly right or right in spirit. Modern prophetic ministry regularly fails at precisely this point and then rewrites the failed word as a misheard impression, which is an admission that the formula was never warranted. The dictionary's position is the cessationist one held across the Reformed tradition: the canon is complete, and God now speaks to His church by His written word, illuminated by His Spirit.

A quieter version of the same abuse is more common and does more damage, because it wears no supernatural claim. It is the preacher, the counsellor, or the parent who attaches divine authority to his own judgment — announcing as God's will what Scripture nowhere says. The remedy is the discipline the formula itself implies: a herald may say thus saith only of what he was actually given. Where Scripture has spoken, speak with all boldness and without apology; where it has not, say so plainly and reason as a fallible man among fallible men.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'amar is the ordinary verb of saying, and koh 'amar YHWH is the messenger formula; ne'um YHWH, rendered saith the LORD, is the oracle marker; Greek uses legei, the present of lego.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'amar (H559) — to say, to speak, to command; the verb of the formula koh 'amar YHWH, thus saith the LORD.

Hebrew ne'um (H5002) — an utterance or oracle; rendered saith the LORD, marking the words as God's own.

Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter, a thing; that which the prophet is given to carry.

Greek legei (G3004) — he saith; the present indicative, used for Christ's living speech in the Gospels.

Saxon sægþ — the Old English third singular present of secgan, to say.

Usage

"Of the LORD swearing by Himself in covenant: By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD (Genesis 22:16)."

"Of a prophet contradicting the national mood: Thus saith the LORD; Deceive not yourselves (Jeremiah 37:9)."

"Of Christ's living speech to His disciples: he saith unto them, Our friend Lazarus sleepeth (John 11:11)."
